column4: text

Each step down a group adds a whole new electron shell, so the outermost electrons sit farther from the nucleus. The extra protons are largely cancelled by the inner shells in between, which shield the outer electrons, so the pull those electrons feel barely grows while their distance does. The atom gets bigger at every step: in group 1, from lithium to caesium.

Across a period, each element adds one proton to the nucleus and one electron to the same outer shell. Electrons in the same shell shield each other poorly, so the effective nuclear charge on the outer electrons rises at every step and draws the whole shell in. Adding electrons does not make the atom bigger here: the stronger pull wins, and the radius shrinks from sodium to chlorine.

Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an atom's outermost electron. Across a period the effective nuclear charge rises and the atom shrinks, so that electron is held more tightly and costs more to remove. It climbs from the alkali metal at the start of the period to the noble gas at its end, with two small dips along the way.

Down a group, the outermost electron sits in a shell farther from the nucleus each time, and the inner shells screen it from most of the added protons. Farther away and better shielded, it is easier to remove, so the first ionization energy falls step by step: in group 1 from lithium to caesium, which is why caesium gives up its electron so readily.

Two dips interrupt the rise across a period. Boron is lower than beryllium because its outer electron is the first in a 2p orbital, which is higher in energy and better shielded than 2s. Oxygen is lower than nitrogen because its fourth 2p electron has to share an orbital, and the repulsion between the paired electrons makes one of them easier to remove. The same two dips come again in period 3, at aluminium and sulfur.

Successive ionization energies rise as each electron is removed, because the ones that remain are held by the same nucleus with less repulsion between them. The big jump comes when the next electron has to come from a full inner shell, much closer to the nucleus and far less shielded. That is why sodium's second ionization energy is about ten times its first: the first empties the outer shell, the second breaks into the neon core.

Electronegativity is how strongly an atom pulls the shared electrons of a bond towards itself. Across a period the nuclear charge felt by the outer shell rises while the atom shrinks, so a bonding pair sits closer to a more strongly charged nucleus. The pull grows at each step, from sodium (0.93) to chlorine (3.16); the noble gases at the end rarely form bonds and usually have no value.

Down a group, the bonding electrons sit in a shell farther from the nucleus and are screened from it by more inner electrons. The nucleus pulls on them less, so electronegativity falls: fluorine is the most electronegative element of all, and each halogen below it pulls a little less.

Fluorine is the most electronegative element because its outer electrons are in the second shell, very close to a nucleus they are poorly shielded from, and it needs only one more electron to fill that shell. A bonding pair shared with fluorine is pulled towards it harder than towards any other atom: 3.98 on the Pauling scale, the highest of any element.

column3: noble gas+unreactive|noble gas+inert|noble gas+stable|noble gas+react|noble gases+unreactive|noble gases+inert|noble gases+stable|noble gases+react
column4: The noble gases have a full outer shell: two electrons for helium, eight for the rest. A full shell is a particularly stable arrangement, so removing an electron costs a great deal of energy, and the noble gases have the highest ionization energies in their periods, while there is nothing to gain from taking one on. With nothing to gain from losing, gaining or sharing electrons, they form compounds only under extreme conditions, such as xenon with fluorine.

column3: alkali metal+reactive|alkali metal+reactivity|alkali metal+react|alkali metals+reactive|alkali metals+react
column4: The alkali metals have a single electron in their outer shell, and losing it leaves the stable arrangement of the noble gas before them. That electron is easy to remove, and easier the farther down the group it sits, because it is farther from the nucleus and better shielded. So reactivity rises down the group: lithium fizzes in water, sodium melts and darts across it, and potassium and the heavier metals ignite.

The halogens are one electron short of a full outer shell, and they react by gaining one. Fluorine's outer shell is closest to the nucleus and least shielded, so it attracts an incoming electron most strongly, which makes it the most reactive. Down the group the outer shell is farther away and better screened, the pull weakens, and the halogens become less reactive: chlorine, then bromine, then iodine.

Metallic character is how readily an element gives up electrons, which is what metals do. It follows ionization energy and electronegativity in reverse: the elements that hold their electrons most loosely are the most metallic. So it increases down a group and decreases across a period, which puts the most metallic elements at the bottom left of the table, the nonmetals at the top right, and the metalloids along the boundary between them.

Across period 3 the melting point rises to a peak at silicon and then collapses. Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metals, held by a sea of electrons that grows stronger as each atom contributes more. Silicon is a giant covalent network, and melting it means breaking strong bonds throughout the solid. Phosphorus, sulfur and chlorine form small separate molecules held together only by weak forces, and argon is single atoms, so their melting points are low.

The alkali metals melt at lower temperatures down the group. Each atom gives a single electron to the metallic bond, and as the atoms grow larger that electron is spread over a bigger volume and held farther from the nuclei, so the bonding weakens. Lithium melts at 180.5 °C and caesium at 28.5 °C, warm enough to melt in a hand.

Density depends on how heavy the atoms are and how closely they pack. Atomic mass rises steadily through the table, but the atoms also shrink across each period, so the densest elements that have been measured are heavy transition metals in the middle of period 6, where a large mass sits in a small, tightly packed atom: osmium and iridium, at about 22.6 g/cm³. The gases at the top and the right are the least dense.

Across the lanthanides, electrons fill the 4f orbitals, which shield the outer electrons poorly. Each added proton therefore draws the outer shell in a little more, and the atoms shrink steadily from lanthanum to lutetium. The effect carries on beyond them: hafnium ends up almost exactly the size of zirconium above it, which is why the two are so hard to separate chemically.

Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. Its outer 6s electrons are pulled unusually close to its heavy nucleus, a relativistic effect of the speed at which they move, so they are reluctant to take part in metallic bonding. With the bonds between its atoms weak, mercury melts at −38.8 °C, far below its neighbours gold and thallium.

In the liquid, the noble gases are held together only by London dispersion forces, which come from fleeting distortions of their electron clouds. Small atoms with few electrons distort least, so helium's forces are the weakest of any element and it boils at −268.9 °C, the lowest boiling point of all. Down the group the atoms grow larger and easier to distort, and the boiling points rise.

Electron affinity is the energy released when an atom gains an electron. Across a period the incoming electron is drawn by a growing effective nuclear charge into a shrinking atom, so more energy is released, and the halogens release the most because one electron completes their outer shell. The rise is uneven: magnesium releases almost none because the new electron must start the 3p subshell, phosphorus little because it must pair up in a half-filled one, and argon none because it must start a new shell.

Across period 3 the boiling point follows the melting point, for the same reason: what has to be broken to boil each element. Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metals whose bonding grows stronger as each atom adds electrons to the shared sea, so aluminium boils at 2470 °C. Silicon's giant covalent network is the peak, at 3265 °C. Phosphorus, sulfur and chlorine boil as small molecules held by weak forces, and argon as single atoms, at −185.8 °C.

Down a group each atom gets heavier faster than it gets bigger, so density mostly rises: lithium is 0.534 g/cm³ and caesium 1.93 g/cm³. The rise is not perfectly smooth. Potassium (0.89 g/cm³) is less dense than sodium (0.97 g/cm³), because at that step the jump in size from one shell to the next outweighs the extra mass. The alkali metals stay light throughout, since each atom gives only one electron to a loosely packed metallic structure.

Across period 4 density climbs from potassium (0.89 g/cm³) to a peak at copper (8.96 g/cm³) and then falls away. Through the transition metals each atom adds mass, while the extra d electrons strengthen the metallic bonding and draw the atoms closer together, so more mass is packed into each cubic centimetre. Once the d subshell is full the bonding weakens again, and the period ends with bromine, a liquid, and krypton, a gas.

Down a group an incoming electron lands in a shell farther from the nucleus and better shielded from it, so less energy is released when it is captured, and electron affinity generally falls. The halogens show it from chlorine through bromine to iodine. The exception is at the top: fluorine releases less than chlorine, because its small outer shell is so crowded that the new electron is pushed back by the ones already there.

Metals conduct heat well because their outer electrons move freely through the whole solid and carry energy as they go, on top of the atomic vibrations that carry heat in every solid. The best conductors are the coinage metals, each with one loosely held outer electron over a full d subshell: silver at 429 W/(m·K), copper at 401 and gold at 318. Nonmetals rely on vibrations alone, and gases conduct worst of all.

column3: hydrogen+specific heat|specific heat+per gram|specific heat+lighter|specific heat+light elements
column4: Specific heat capacity is the heat needed to warm one gram by one kelvin. For most solid elements the heat needed per atom is about the same, roughly 25 J per mole per kelvin, so the heat per gram depends mainly on how many atoms a gram holds. Light atoms mean many atoms to the gram: lithium needs 3.58 J/(g·K), sodium 1.23 and caesium only 0.24. Hydrogen, the lightest of all, has the highest value of any element, 14.3 J/(g·K).

The work function is the energy needed to pull an electron out of a metal's surface, which is what light does in the photoelectric effect. Down group 1 the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and better shielded, so it escapes more easily: lithium's work function is 2.9 eV and caesium's only 2.14 eV, low enough for visible light to free electrons. That is why caesium is used in photocells and light detectors.

The halogens are held together as liquids and solids only by London forces between their two-atom molecules. Down the group the molecules have more electrons in larger, more easily distorted clouds, so the forces grow stronger and more energy is needed to separate the molecules. That is why fluorine and chlorine are gases at room temperature, bromine is a liquid that boils at 58.8 °C, and iodine is a solid that melts at 113.7 °C.

Chlorine releases more energy than fluorine when it gains an electron, although fluorine attracts bonding electrons more strongly. Fluorine's outer shell is the second, very small and already holding seven electrons close together, so a new electron arriving there is pushed back hard by the others. Chlorine's third shell is roomier, the repulsion is smaller, and more of the nucleus's pull is released as energy.

column3: electron affinity+zero|electron affinity+nitrogen|electron affinity+beryllium|electron affinity+magnesium|electron affinity+noble gas|electron affinity+noble gases
column4: Some atoms release no energy when they gain an electron, and the app records their electron affinity as 0. Beryllium and magnesium have a full s subshell, so a new electron has to start the higher-energy p subshell. The noble gases have a full shell, so it would have to start a new shell altogether. Nitrogen's half-full p subshell is unusually stable and an added electron must pair up, so nitrogen releases almost nothing.

column3: transition metals+radius|transition metals+radii|transition metal+radii|transition metals+size|transition metals+similar size|transition metal+radius|transition metals+atomic radius
column4: Across the transition metals the atoms change size far less than across the rest of a period: in period 4 the radius falls 49 pm from potassium to calcium alone, but only 26 pm from vanadium to copper. Each added electron goes into the inner 3d subshell rather than the outer 4s, and those inner electrons shield the outer ones from each new proton almost as fast as the nuclear charge grows. With the outer electrons feeling nearly the same pull, the radius hardly moves.

Across the transition metals the first ionization energy rises only slowly: in period 4 it goes from 6.56 eV at scandium to 7.73 eV at copper, while the elements after them climb from 6.00 eV at gallium to 14.0 eV at krypton. The electron removed first is a 4s electron, and the 3d electrons being added beneath it shield it from most of each new proton's pull. Zinc stands out at 9.39 eV, because removing its electron breaks a full 4s pair above a full 3d subshell.

Helium has the highest first ionization energy of any element, 24.6 eV. Its two electrons sit in the first shell, as close to the nucleus as electrons get, with no inner electrons to shield them from its two protons, and removing one breaks up a full shell, the most stable arrangement there is. Down group 18 the outer electrons sit farther out, and by xenon the value has fallen to about half, 12.1 eV.

Ionization energy falls sharply from each noble gas to the alkali metal after it: from 21.6 eV at neon to 5.14 eV at sodium. Neon's electrons fill the second shell under a nuclear charge of ten. Sodium's eleventh electron has to start the third shell, farther out, with ten inner electrons shielding it from almost all of the nucleus. The same drop opens every period, which is why the alkali metals give up their electron so readily.

Where the big jump in successive ionization energies comes tells you how many outer electrons an atom has, and so its group. Aluminium's first three electrons come from the third shell and cost steadily more; the fourth has to come from the full second shell beneath, and the cost leaps. Three easy electrons and then a jump means three outer electrons: group 13. Sodium jumps after one electron and magnesium after two.

Chromium is written 3d⁵ 4s¹ rather than 3d⁴ 4s², and copper 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ rather than 3d⁹ 4s². In these atoms the 4s and 3d levels lie very close together, so small effects decide where the electrons go. A half-full or full d subshell spreads the electrons evenly and lowers the repulsion between them, which outweighs the small cost of moving one electron up from 4s. Molybdenum, silver and gold follow the same pattern.

Tungsten melts at 3422 °C, higher than any other metal. Its six outer electrons, four 5d and two 6s, can all take part in metallic bonding, about as many as a metal can usefully share, and a half-filled d band makes the bonds especially strong. Its heavy, compact atoms in a tightly bonded crystal add to it. Its neighbours rhenium (3186 °C), osmium and tantalum, with similar numbers of bonding electrons, follow close behind.

Gallium melts at 29.8 °C, so a piece held in the hand turns liquid. Its solid is unusual: instead of a closely packed metal, the atoms pair up into Ga₂ units held by strong bonds, with only weak metallic bonding between the pairs, and that structure comes apart easily. Once melted, gallium stays liquid up to about 2400 °C, one of the longest liquid ranges of any element.

Transition metals have high melting points because they bond with their d electrons as well as their s electrons. In period 4 the melting point climbs from 63.5 °C at potassium to about 1900 °C at vanadium and chromium, where about half the d subshell is used for bonding. Past the middle the extra d electrons start to pair up and add less to the bonding, so melting points fall again, down to 419.5 °C at zinc, whose d subshell is full.

The group 2 metals melt far higher than the group 1 metals beside them: calcium at 842 °C against potassium's 63.5 °C. Each atom gives two electrons to the metallic bonding instead of one, and its nucleus has an extra proton, so the ions are smaller, more highly charged and more strongly held by the electron sea. Down the group the melting points do not fall in a smooth line, because the metals crystallise in different structures.

The alkaline earth metals react by losing their two outer electrons, which costs more energy than losing the single electron of the alkali metal beside them: calcium's first ionization energy is 6.11 eV against potassium's 4.34 eV. So they are less reactive than group 1. Down the group the outer electrons are farther out and better shielded, ionization energies fall and reactivity rises: beryllium barely reacts with water, magnesium only with steam, calcium steadily and barium vigorously.

Gold and platinum hardly react because they hold their outer electrons unusually tightly. Gold's first ionization energy, 9.23 eV, is well above silver's 7.58 eV, although gold sits lower in the group. In so heavy an atom the inner electrons move fast enough for relativity to matter: the 6s orbital is drawn in close to the nucleus, and its electron is harder to remove or share. That is why gold does not tarnish in air while silver and copper do.

Heavy elements in groups 13 to 15 often use fewer electrons than their group number suggests: thallium forms Tl⁺ more readily than Tl³⁺, and lead prefers Pb²⁺ to Pb⁴⁺. Their outer s pair is held unusually tightly, drawn in by a large nuclear charge that the filled d and f subshells shield poorly, and by relativistic effects. The card shows it: lead's first ionization energy, 7.42 eV, is higher than that of tin above it, 7.34 eV, against the trend down the group.

Lithium resembles magnesium, beryllium resembles aluminium, and boron resembles silicon, more than each resembles the element below it. Moving right across a period raises electronegativity and shrinks the atom; moving down a group lowers electronegativity and enlarges it. A diagonal step does both and they roughly cancel, so the diagonal pairs have similar sizes and charge densities, and similar chemistry: lithium and magnesium both form nitrides when burned in air, for example.

Hydrogen sits above the alkali metals because, like them, it has one electron in its outer shell. It behaves very differently: it is a gas of H₂ molecules, its electronegativity is 2.20 against lithium's 0.98, and its first ionization energy, 13.6 eV, is close to that of the nonmetals. It also needs only one more electron to fill its shell, as a halogen does, so some tables show it above fluorine as well, or on its own.

Helium has two electrons, 1s², which by configuration alone would put it beside beryllium in group 2. It sits in group 18 because it behaves as a noble gas: its two electrons fill the first shell completely, and that full shell makes it the least reactive element of all, with the highest ionization energy in the table. The table groups elements by behaviour, and a full outer shell matters more than how many electrons fill it.

The heavier noble gases can form compounds because their outer electrons are farther from the nucleus. Xenon's first ionization energy, 12.1 eV, is about half of helium's, low enough for the most electronegative elements to pull electrons from it. In 1962 xenon was made to react with platinum hexafluoride, and xenon fluorides and oxides followed. Helium and neon, holding their electrons far more tightly, form no stable compounds.

Carbon forms more compounds than any other element because of how it bonds. With four outer electrons it makes four strong covalent bonds, and with a middling electronegativity, 2.55, it shares electrons rather than giving them up or taking them. Carbon–carbon bonds are strong enough to build long chains and rings that stay stable, and carbon bonds well to hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and itself, in single, double and triple bonds.

The metalloids, boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony and tellurium, sit on the border between metals and nonmetals, and their properties fall in between. Their electronegativities are middling, about 1.9 to 2.2, so their outer electrons are neither free to roam as in a metal nor tightly locked into bonds as in a nonmetal. A little energy frees some of them to conduct, which makes silicon and germanium semiconductors whose conductivity rises with temperature.

The lanthanides are chemically very alike because the electrons they add go into the 4f subshell, buried inside the atom beneath the 5s, 5p and 6s electrons. The outer electrons that take part in reactions are the same for all of them, and nearly all form +3 ions of similar size. That is why they occur together in the same ores and were so hard to tell apart: separating them took repeated crystallisations and, later, ion-exchange columns.

Shielding is the way inner electrons screen the outer ones from the nucleus. An outer electron feels the pull of all the protons, less the repulsion of the electrons between it and the nucleus; what is left is the effective nuclear charge. Inner shells shield well, while electrons in the same shell barely shield each other. That one idea explains most periodic trends: across a period the effective charge grows and atoms shrink, while down a group a new shell keeps it roughly level as the distance grows.

Elements in the same group behave alike because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, and those are the electrons that take part in reactions. Lithium, sodium and potassium each have one outer electron that they lose easily, so all three react with water to give hydrogen and an alkaline solution. What changes down the group is how tightly that electron is held, which is why the reactions grow more vigorous.

The table is periodic because electrons fill shells, and properties depend mostly on the outermost one. Each period fills a shell from one electron to full; the next element starts a new shell with one electron, and the pattern repeats. So atomic radius, ionization energy and electronegativity rise and fall in waves, and the elements at the same point of each wave, a group, behave alike. Mendeleev saw the repetition in 1869, before anyone knew of electrons.

The noble gases usually have no electronegativity value. Electronegativity describes how strongly an atom pulls on the electrons it shares in a bond, and helium, neon and argon form no stable bonds to measure it in. Krypton and xenon do form a few compounds, so values have been estimated for them, 3.00 and 2.6 in the app's data, but they are less certain than for other elements.

A bond is polar when its two atoms differ in electronegativity: the shared electrons spend more time near the atom that pulls harder, which takes a slight negative charge and leaves the other slightly positive. In water, oxygen (3.44) pulls the electrons away from hydrogen (2.20), so each O–H bond is polar. Two identical atoms share equally, and a difference above about 1.8 means the electron is effectively transferred and the bond is ionic.

column3: ionic bond|ionic bonds|ionic compound|ionic compounds|ionic bonding
column4: Metals and nonmetals form ionic compounds because one gives up electrons easily and the other takes them readily. Sodium has a low electronegativity, 0.93, and loses its outer electron at little cost; chlorine, at 3.16, gains one and completes its shell. The difference is so large that the electron is transferred rather than shared, and the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are held in a crystal by the strong attraction of opposite charges.

column3: metals+positive ions|metal+positive ions|metals+cations|metals+lose electrons|metal+lose electrons|form cations
column4: Metals form positive ions because their outer electrons are easy to remove. They have few outer electrons, loosely held, so losing them costs less energy than is returned when the ions are surrounded by water or packed into a crystal, and the ion left behind has the stable shell of the noble gas before it. Across period 3 the cost rises steeply, from 5.14 eV for sodium's first electron to 15.8 eV for argon's, which is why the metals sit on the left.

Metals conduct electricity because their outer electrons are not tied to any one atom. In a metal each atom gives its outer electrons to a sea shared by the whole crystal, and a voltage sets that sea drifting. The same free electrons carry heat, which is why the best electrical conductors, silver and copper, are also the best conductors of heat: 429 and 401 W/(m·K) on the card. Nonmetals hold their electrons in bonds and conduct poorly.

column3: atomic mass+whole number|atomic masses+whole numbers|atomic mass+decimal|atomic mass+not whole|atomic mass+average
column4: Atomic masses are not whole numbers because most elements are mixtures of isotopes, and the table gives the average weighted by how common each one is. Chlorine is about three-quarters chlorine-35 and one-quarter chlorine-37, so its atomic mass is 35.45. Even a single isotope is not quite a whole number: protons and neutrons weigh slightly more than one unit each, and some mass is lost as binding energy when the nucleus forms.

Atomic radius jumps at the start of every period: neon is 38 pm and sodium, the next element, 190 pm. Sodium's eleventh electron has to begin the third shell, farther from the nucleus, and the ten electrons beneath it shield it from almost all of the nuclear charge. Across the period the radius then shrinks again as the shell fills, so the radius follows a sawtooth through the table.
